opus-5.5.text:
I think Miaoya is a really interesting case. The experience itself is simple: you upload a few photos of yourself, pay a small fee, something like 9.9 yuan, and you get a set of very polished, studio-style portraits. That simplicity is a big part of why it took off. Users don't need to understand Stable Diffusion, LoRA, or prompts. They just get a nice picture of themselves they can share on WeChat Moments, and that shareability drove the viral loop.

From a technical point of view, it isn't fundamentally new. Personalized image generation, where you fine-tune or condition a model on a few photos of one person, has been around in the open-source community for a while. What Miaoya did well was productization: packaging the technology in a form ordinary people could use, at a price low enough that it became an impulse purchase.

When it first went viral, though, I was thinking about two things.

The first is cost and infrastructure. Because each user effectively needs some personalized processing, the compute load scales directly with users. When it suddenly became popular, there were queues, people waiting hours or longer for their photos. That's a classic sign that AI applications are constrained by GPU capacity and serving efficiency in a way traditional internet apps aren't. A normal mini-program might cost almost nothing per extra user. Here, every additional user consumes real GPU time. So doing the infra and cost math well matters a lot if you want to survive a viral spike.

The second question is retention. Making a set of portraits is a very satisfying one-time experience, but how often do you need new ones? Maybe once, maybe a few times. After the novelty wears off, it's hard to see daily or even monthly usage. So my view at the time was that it was a great demonstration of consumer demand for AI, but whether it becomes a lasting product depends on finding a repeat use case, not just a one-off wow moment.

So overall I'm positive about it. It showed that generative AI can reach mass consumers in China very quickly when the product is right. But it also illustrates the core challenges for AI applications: the economics of inference and the need for sustained, recurring value beyond the initial viral hit.

r001.rationale: The candidate says users upload “a few photos,” but does not identify a 20-photo requirement or characterize it as a substantial input burden.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Miaoya was a genuinely interesting moment, and I'd separate what it got right from what it tells us about where the industry is.

What it got right was the product framing. Technically, there was nothing in Miaoya that the AI community hadn't seen before. It was essentially LoRA fine-tuning on top of Stable Diffusion, plus a reasonably careful pipeline for face consistency and prompt templates. Anyone who had played with Civitai or DreamBooth in 2022 knew the recipe. But Miaoya did something researchers usually don't bother to do: they picked one narrow use case, the professional headshot, and made the whole experience feel finished. You upload twenty photos, you pay 9.9 yuan, you wait, you get something you'd actually put on your profile. No prompts, no parameters, no sliders. That constraint is the product.

The second thing I'd point to is the wait time. People made fun of the multi-hour queue, but I actually think it did two things for them. One, it was a real compute constraint, because fine-tuning per user is expensive and they clearly weren't provisioned for that kind of spike. Two, it accidentally created anticipation. There's a bit of a "developing film" feeling to it. I don't think they planned that, but it shows that latency isn't always the enemy of experience.

Where I'd be more cautious is on durability. Miaoya is a good example of what I'd call a "single-shot" AI product. The use case is strong but it's not frequent. How many times a year do you need a new headshot? Once you've generated yours, the mini-program has done its job, and there's not an obvious reason to come back. So you see a very steep curve up and then a steep curve down, and the question becomes whether you can convert that burst of attention into something with retention. Several companies have tried the same playbook since, and most of them hit the same wall.

The deeper lesson for me, and this is something I think about a lot at Lepton, is on the infrastructure side. Miaoya's biggest headache during those few days wasn't the model, it was serving. They had to scale GPU capacity very fast, handle a fine-tuning job per user rather than one shared model, and keep costs under the 9.9 yuan they were charging. That's a much harder engineering problem than the demo suggests. A lot of AI applications are going to look like this: thin on novel research, heavy on making inference and fine-tuning cheap, fast, and reliable at scale. The teams that win will be the ones who treat that part seriously rather than as an afterthought.

So my overall view is positive. It's a reminder that in this wave, a good product instinct plus solid engineering can create real consumer moments without a frontier model behind it. Whether any single one of these moments becomes a lasting business is a separate question, and I think Miaoya itself is still working on that answer.

r001.rationale: The response says users upload twenty photos, but presents this as part of the product flow and does not characterize the requirement as a substantial input burden.

astra-6.text:
I think Miaoya Camera offers a very intuitive way for people to experience generative AI. You don’t have to understand the technology or learn how to write prompts. You give it photos of yourself, and the result is something personal that you can immediately appreciate and share.

What interests me is the gap between demonstrating a capability and making it into a product. “AI can generate images” is a capability. “I can get a set of portraits of myself” is a concrete reason to use it. Narrowing the experience to that specific need can actually make the technology more compelling.

Of course, trying something because it’s novel is different from continuing to use it. The longer-term question is whether the results are consistently good enough, and whether people have a reason to come back. But as an introduction to what generative AI can do, that kind of simple, personal experience is powerful.

r001.rationale: The response says users provide photos of themselves, but does not mention that 20 photos are required or characterize that requirement as a substantial burden.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Miaoya Camera is interesting because it turns an AI capability into a very concrete consumer experience. You don’t have to understand the model or figure out how to write a prompt—you upload your photos, and the product helps you get a set of portraits. The value is easy to understand, and the results are something people naturally want to share.

There’s still friction, though. You have to choose and upload photos, wait for the results, and accept that some images may look more like you than others. That gap between an impressive result and a consistently satisfying experience is where a lot of product work happens.

So I’d see its popularity as a promising signal. It shows that people will try AI when it’s packaged around something they want. Whether that becomes a lasting business depends on what brings them back after the initial curiosity.

r001.rationale: The response mentions choosing and uploading photos as friction, but it does not state that 20 photos are required or characterize that quantity as a substantial input burden.
